extracted.intended_audience: writers, comedians, students, and general readers learning differences between humor/rhetorical devices
extracted.subtask_description: A short tutorial-style rubric for identifying and distinguishing irony, sarcasm, satire, and paradox in writing or speech. Useful for creators and readers who need to label, write, or critique humor and rhetorical devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irony (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Something happens that is the opposite of what was expected. Juxtaposition of what appears on the surface vs. what is actually the case. Neutral by definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irony denotes a gap between appearance and reality; it is not inherently mocking. Can be situational, verbal, dramatic, or cosmic (see types). Useful to note that irony can be unintentional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sarcasm (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: An ironic remark meant to mock by saying something different than what the speaker really means. Caustic, often insulting. Sarcasm requires intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sarcasm is a sub-type of verbal irony with an explicit mocking/insulting aim. Tone tends to be biting; the speaker's intent to mock distinguishes it from neutral irony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of humor, irony, exaggeration, or ridicule to expose and criticize stupidity or vices. Always has a target/agenda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire combines devices (irony, exaggeration, ridicule) with a clear target and critical purpose — it's agenda-driven rather than merely ironic. Evaluate by identifying the target and the critical point being made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradox (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: An apparent contradiction that contains truth. Not strictly humorous but humor-adjacent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paradoxical statements reveal deeper truths despite surface contradiction; they may produce wry amusement but are not primarily about mocking or targeting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verbal Irony (type)
rubrics_metrics.description: Saying something different from what you really mean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize by mismatch between literal wording and intended meaning. Sarcasm is a caustic, intentional form of verbal irony; verbal irony can also be gentle or neutral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situational Irony (type)
rubrics_metrics.description: The opposite of what's expected actually happens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for outcomes that contradict expectations (example: a fire station burns down). This is often applied to events/situations rather than people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic Irony (type)
rubrics_metrics.description: The audience knows something the characters don't.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creates tension and often humor because of the audience's superior knowledge; common in plays, films, and stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cosmic Irony (type)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fate or some higher power orchestrates an ironic outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribute the ironic outcome to fate/forces beyond control; used to highlight human limitations or destiny's cruelty/absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface vs. actual meaning (core test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is there a gap between surface and actual meaning?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary diagnostic for irony and sarcasm: identify whether the literal words/appearance differ from the intended or actual state of affairs. If no gap, it's not ironic/sarcastic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intentionality (core test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is it intentional? (Irony can be unintentional; sarcasm requires intention.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the speaker/creator intended the gap to be noticed as mocking or critical. Intent separates neutral/unintentional irony from biting sarcasm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target clarity (core test)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sarcasm and satire typically have identifiable targets (people, institutions, ideas). Satire in particular 'always has a target/agenda' — check whether the device is aimed at criticizing something specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone (core test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the tone biting (sarcasm) or neutral (irony)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess emotional quality: biting/caustic tone signals sarcasm; neutral or simply incongruous tone suggests irony. Tone helps distinguish intent and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience perception (core test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the audience perceive the gap?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irony/sarcasm often depends on the audience recognizing the discrepancy. If the audience doesn't perceive the gap, the intended effect (humor, mockery, critique) may fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situations vs. people (heuristic distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Situations are ironic; people are sarcastic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this rule of thumb when labeling examples: if the incongruity is in events/ outcomes, call it irony; if it's in a person's remark aimed at someone/something, consider sarcasm.
